pumac-2017-number-theory-b-01.title: Fewest digits, smallest leading digit (official method)
pumac-2017-number-theory-b-01.body:
To be smallest, a number should have as few digits as possible, and then the smallest possible leading digit; so the digits after the first should be $9$s.

- $1\le n\le9$: $a_n=n$, sum $45$.
- $10\le n\le18$: two digits, $a_n=\overline{(n-9)9}=10(n-9)+9=10n-81$: $19,29,\dots,99$, sum $10\cdot126-81\cdot9=1260-729=531$.
- $a_{19}=199$, $a_{20}=299$.

Total: $45+531+199+299=1074$.

**Answer: 1074**

pumac-2017-number-theory-b-01.title: List them
pumac-2017-number-theory-b-01.body:
$1,2,\dots,9$ (sum $45$); $19,29,39,49,59,69,79,89,99$ (sum $9\cdot59=531$); $199$; $299$. Each is smallest because with fewer digits the digit sum is at most $9\times$(number of digits), and the leading digit is as small as allowed. Sum $=45+531+498=1074$.

**Answer: 1074**

pumac-2017-number-theory-b-02.title: Repunits (official method)
pumac-2017-number-theory-b-02.body:
Let $f(n)=\underbrace{nn\cdots n}_{n}=n\cdot R_n$ where $R_n=\underbrace{11\cdots1}_{n}$. If $m\mid n$, then $R_m\mid R_n$ (split the $n$ ones into blocks of $m$) and $m\mid n$, so $f(m)\mid f(n)$.

Conversely, if $a\nmid b$ then $f(a)\nmid f(b)$. The key factors: $11\mid R_n$ iff $n$ is even, $37\mid R_n$ iff $3\mid n$ (and $f(3)=333=9\cdot37$), $101\mid R_n$ iff $4\mid n$ (and $f(4)=4\cdot11\cdot101$); for $a\ge5$ the only multiple of $a$ in $\{a+1,\dots,9\}$ is at most $2a$, and dividing the few remaining candidates (e.g. $55555\nmid 666666$) confirms the rule. Also $f(2)=22$ needs $b$ even since $f(b)$ is even only for even $b$.

So we count pairs $a<b$ in $\{1,\dots,9\}$ with $a\mid b$:
$b=2:1$; $b=3:1$; $b=4:2$; $b=5:1$; $b=6:3$; $b=7:1$; $b=8:3$; $b=9:2$. Total $14$.

**Answer: 14**

pumac-2017-number-theory-b-02.title: Direct check
pumac-2017-number-theory-b-02.body:
There are only $\binom92=36$ pairs; dividing each $f(b)$ by each smaller $f(a)$ (e.g. by computer) shows exactly the pairs with $a\mid b$ work: $(1,b)$ for $b=2..9$ ($8$ pairs), $(2,4),(2,6),(2,8)$, $(3,6),(3,9)$, $(4,8)$ — that is $8+3+2+1=14$. For instance $22\nmid333$ (odd), $333\nmid4444$, $4444\mid88888888$ ($=2\cdot4444\cdot10001$).

**Answer: 14**

pumac-2017-number-theory-b-03.title: Bounds and constructions
pumac-2017-number-theory-b-03.body:
Each operation reduces the count by $2$, so after $1008$ operations one number remains. Think of each number on the board as coming from a set of original numbers (its "leaves"): an original number has itself as its only leaf, and a new number has as leaves the union of the leaves of the three numbers it replaced. Different numbers on the board have disjoint leaf sets.

**Upper bound.** Claim: every number $v$ on the board is at most the largest of its leaves. True for originals. If $v=1+\operatorname{median}(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ with $v_i\le\max L_i$, then the median is at most the second largest of $\max L_1,\max L_2,\max L_3$. These are distinct integers (disjoint leaf sets), so the second largest is at most $\max L-1$, giving $v\le\max L$. Hence the final number is at most $2017$.

**Lower bound.** Similarly, a created number $v$ satisfies $v\ge\min L+2$: the median of the $v_i$ is at least the second smallest of the $v_i\ge\min L_i$, which is at least $\min L+1$ (again distinct integers). So the final number is at least $1+2=3$.

**Constructions.** For $m=3$: first do $1007$ operations using only numbers from $\{3,\dots,2017\}$ (new numbers stay $\ge3$), leaving $1$, $2$ and some $x\ge3$; the last operation gives $1+2=3$. For $M=2017$: do $1007$ operations within $\{1,\dots,2015\}$ (new numbers are $1+$median $\le2015$), leaving some $y\le2015$, $2016$ and $2017$; the last operation gives $1+2016=2017$.

So $M-m=2017-3=2014$. (The official solution argues the same bounds directly: $2$ would need two numbers $\le1$, and a value above $2017$ would need a $2017$ and a larger number at the same time.)

**Answer: 2014**

pumac-2017-number-theory-b-03.title: Check small boards
pumac-2017-number-theory-b-03.body:
Run an exhaustive search for the boards $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with small odd $n$ (trying every choice of triple at every step). For $n=5,7,9,11$ the largest possible final number is $n$ and the smallest is $3$, exactly the pattern $M=n$, $m=3$ proved above. For $n=2017$: $M-m=2017-3=2014$.

**Answer: 2014**

pumac-2017-number-theory-b-04.title: Two distinct primes are needed and enough (official method)
pumac-2017-number-theory-b-04.body:
$a_2$ shares a prime $p$ with $a_1$ and a prime $q$ with $a_3$, while $\gcd(a_1,a_3)=1$, so $p\ne q$: $a_2$ has at least two distinct prime factors.

Conversely, any $a_2$ with two distinct prime factors $p,q$ works: take $a_1=p$, $a_3=q\,r_3$, and then $a_n=r_{n-1}r_n$ for $n\geq4$, using fresh primes $r_3,r_4,\dots$ different from all prime factors of $a_2$ — then consecutive terms share exactly one prime and non-consecutive terms are coprime.

The smallest positive integers with at least two distinct prime factors are $6,10,12,14,15,\dots$ So the answer is $6+10+12+14=42$.

**Answer: 42**

pumac-2017-number-theory-b-04.title: List candidates
pumac-2017-number-theory-b-04.body:
Check $2,3,\dots$: prime powers ($2,3,4,5,7,8,9,11,13$) are impossible because then $a_1$ and $a_3$ would both share that single prime and so $\gcd(a_1,a_3)>1$. The first non-prime-powers are $6=2\cdot3$, $10=2\cdot5$, $12=2^2\cdot3$, $14=2\cdot7$, each realisable as above. Sum: $42$.

**Answer: 42**

pumac-2017-number-theory-b-05.title: Factor the bigness (official method)
pumac-2017-number-theory-b-05.body:
For sides $a,b,c$: $abc+2(ab+bc+ca)+4(a+b+c)=(a+2)(b+2)(c+2)-8$. So $N$ is a bigness iff $N+8=xyz$ with integers $x,y,z\ge3$.

Products of three integers $\ge3$, in increasing order: $27,36,45,48,54,60,63,64,72,75,80,81,\dots$ ($3\cdot3\cdot3$, $3\cdot3\cdot4$, $3\cdot3\cdot5$, $3\cdot4\cdot4$, $3\cdot3\cdot6$, $3\cdot4\cdot5$, $3\cdot3\cdot7$, $4\cdot4\cdot4$, ...). The first two consecutive values are $63=3\cdot3\cdot7$ and $64=4\cdot4\cdot4$. So $N+8=63$, $N=55$ (prisms $1\times1\times5$ and $2\times2\times2$).

Check: $1\cdot1\cdot5=5$, surface $2(1+5+5)=22$, edges $4\cdot7=28$: total $55$. And $2\times2\times2$: $8+24+24=56$.

**Answer: 55**

pumac-2017-number-theory-b-05.title: Brute-force list
pumac-2017-number-theory-b-05.body:
Listing the bigness of all small integer prisms gives the values $19,28,37,40,46,52,55,56,64,\dots$ The first pair of consecutive integers is $55,56$, so $N=55$.

**Answer: 55**

pumac-2017-number-theory-b-06.title: $b_n-1$ must be a multiple of every $m\le n$
pumac-2017-number-theory-b-06.body:
**Sufficient.** In base $b$, $N\equiv s_b(N)\pmod{b-1}$ (because $b\equiv1$). So if every $m\le n$ divides $b-1$, then $m\mid s_b(N)$ implies $m\mid N$.

**Necessary.** Let $b\ge2$ have the property. First, $b>n$: otherwise take $m=b$ and $N=2b-1$, written $\overline{1\,(b-1)}$ in base $b$, with digit sum $b$; but $b\nmid2b-1$. Now for each $m\le n$ (so $m-1<b$), $N=b+(m-1)$ is written $\overline{1\,(m-1)}$ with digit sum $m$, so $m\mid b+m-1$, i.e. $m\mid b-1$. Thus $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,n)\mid b-1$. (A computer search for small $n$ agrees: $b_2=3$, $b_3=7$, $b_4=13$, $b_5=b_6=61$, $b_7=421$.)

So $b_n=1+\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\dots,n)$. Going from $25$ to $36$, the lcm gains the prime powers $27$ (an extra factor $3$), $29$, $31$ and $32$ (an extra factor $2$):
$$\frac{b_{36}}{b_{25}}=\frac{1+\operatorname{lcm}(1..36)}{1+\operatorname{lcm}(1..25)}\approx\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(1..36)}{\operatorname{lcm}(1..25)}=3\cdot29\cdot31\cdot2=5394,$$
and the error is far less than $\frac12$ (the true ratio is $5393.99999998\ldots$).

**Answer: 5394**

pumac-2017-number-theory-b-06.title: Official formulation
pumac-2017-number-theory-b-06.body:
The official solution states $b_n=1+\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,n')$, where $n'$ is the largest prime power not exceeding $n$ (this lcm equals $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,n)$). Here $36'=32$ and $25'=25$, and
$$\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,32)}{\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,25)}=\frac{2^5\cdot3^3\cdot5^2\cdots31}{2^4\cdot3^2\cdot5^2\cdots23}=2\cdot3\cdot29\cdot31=5394.$$

**Answer: 5394**

pumac-2017-number-theory-b-07.title: Work modulo 3, 5, 7 (official method)
pumac-2017-number-theory-b-07.body:
Note $p(x)=(x^2-16)(x^2+10)$. Write $x=n-30$, so $q=|p(x)p(x+60)|$; since $60$ is divisible by $3$ and $5$, $x\equiv x+60$ modulo $3$ and $5$.

- **Mod 3:** $p(x)\equiv x^4-1$, which is $0$ iff $3\nmid x$, i.e. $3\nmid n$. So $a_n=3$ when $n\not\equiv0\pmod 3$.
- **Mod 5** (with $3\mid x$): $p(x)\equiv x^4-x^2=x^2(x^2-1)$, which is $0$ iff $x\equiv0,\pm1\pmod5$. With $x=n-30\equiv n$: $a_n=5$ when $3\mid n$ and $n\equiv0,\pm1\pmod5$.

  (The official solution writes $x=3y$ and gets $y\equiv0,\pm2$, which is the same condition since $3y\equiv0,\pm1\iff y\equiv0,\pm2\pmod5$.)
- **Mod 7:** $p(x)\equiv(x^2-2)(x^2-4)$ and $x+60\equiv x+4$. The squares mod $7$ are $0,1,2,4$. Running through $x=0,\dots,6$, either $x^2$ or $(x+4)^2$ is always $2$ or $4$, so $7\mid q$ always. Thus $a_n=7$ in the remaining cases.

So $a_n=3$ if $3\nmid n$; $a_n=5$ if $3\mid n$ and $n\equiv0,\pm1\pmod5$; otherwise $a_n=7$. The exact count is done in the second approach: $1345$ threes, $403$ fives and $269$ sevens, for a total of $7933$.

**Answer: 7933**

pumac-2017-number-theory-b-07.title: Exact count
pumac-2017-number-theory-b-07.body:
From the first approach: $a_n=3$ if $3\nmid n$; $a_n=5$ if $3\mid n$ and $n\equiv0,1,4\pmod5$; otherwise $a_n=7$. (Also $q(n)=0$ only when $n-30$ or $n+30$ is $\pm4$, i.e. $n\in\{26,34\}$, both not multiples of $3$, so $a_n=3$ as the rule says.)

- $3\nmid n$: $2017-672=1345$ values.
- $n=3k$ ($k=1..672$) with $3k\equiv0,1,4\pmod5\iff k\equiv0,2,3\pmod5$: for $k=1..670$ there are $3\cdot134=402$, and $k=671\equiv1$, $672\equiv2$ add one more: $403$.
- The rest: $672-403=269$ values with $a_n=7$.

Sum: $3\cdot1345+5\cdot403+7\cdot269=4035+2015+1883=7933$. A direct computer evaluation of all $2017$ terms also gives $7933$.

**Answer: 7933**

pumac-2017-number-theory-b-08.title: A covering system (official method)
pumac-2017-number-theory-b-08.body:
Powers of $2$ are periodic modulo small primes: period $2$ mod $3$, $4$ mod $5$, $3$ mod $7$, $12$ mod $13$. If $p\mid N\cdot2^r+1$, then $p\mid N\cdot2^{n}+1$ for all $n\equiv r$ modulo the period. So we want to choose $N$ modulo $3,5,7,13$ so that every residue $r\not\equiv0\pmod{12}$ is "covered" by one of these primes, while $r\equiv0$ need not be.

- Mod $3$ (period $2$) must avoid $r=0$, so it covers the odd residues $1,3,5,7,9,11$.
- Mod $5$ (period $4$), avoiding $0$ and not duplicating: covers $2,6,10$.
- Remaining: $4,8$. Mod $7$ (period $3$) covers one of the classes $\{1,4,7,10\}$ or $\{2,5,8,11\}$, and mod $13$ covers the last one ($8$ or $4$).

The two systems are
$$2N\equiv-1\ (3),\ 4N\equiv-1\ (5),\ 4N\equiv-1\ (7),\ 2^8N\equiv-1\ (13)\ \Rightarrow\ N\equiv556\pmod{1365},$$
$$2N\equiv-1\ (3),\ 4N\equiv-1\ (5),\ 2N\equiv-1\ (7),\ 2^4N\equiv-1\ (13)\ \Rightarrow\ N\equiv901\pmod{1365}.$$
(Check $N=556$: $1+556\cdot2^n$ is divisible by $3$ for odd $n$, by $5$ for $n\equiv2\pmod4$, by $7$ for $n\equiv1\pmod3$ and by $13$ for $n\equiv8\pmod{12}$ — every $n\not\equiv0\pmod{12}$ is covered, and the number is larger than the prime dividing it.)

So $N=556$ works, and the official answer is that it is the least such $N$.

**Answer: 556**

pumac-2017-number-theory-b-08.title: Ruling out smaller $N$ by computer
pumac-2017-number-theory-b-08.body:
For every $N<556$, search for some $n\not\equiv0\pmod{12}$ with $1+N\cdot2^n$ prime. Almost all $N$ have such an $n$ below $400$. The stubborn ones are $N=47,94,188,376$ (all $47\cdot2^k$), $241$, $346$, $383$ and $451$, but primes exist for them too: $47\cdot2^{583}+1$ (giving $n=583,582,581,580$ for $47,94,188,376$), $241\cdot2^{5528}+1$, $173\cdot2^{23313}+1$ (so $n=23312$ for $N=346$), $383\cdot2^{6393}+1$ and $451\cdot2^{6740}+1$ are (probable) primes, and none of these exponents is a multiple of $12$. Hence no $N<556$ works, and $N=556$ is the least.

**Answer: 556**
